**Verdict:** Raise your prices first. Hormozi would almost certainly not tell a 4-person agency to take on more clients at the current rate. He'd tell you to charge more, aim at the clients who value your work most, and grow volume only after that.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: high). He never discussed an agency of your exact size. But his pricing rule appears in three sources, and he has applied it directly to small service businesses.

**How we get there**
1. **The nearest case he addressed.** An HVAC-cleaning owner raised prices 23% and closed *more* deals. Hormozi then proposed another 10% raise: "some of the biggest levers that exist in the business is simply charging more because people actually believe you can deliver the service now." ([yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4 @ 8:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=486s)). The vault notes he aims this at owners under roughly $3–5M in revenue. At about $420k a year, you're well below that.
2. **The rule behind it** (from his thinking page). Charge more, and sell to whoever values it most. He also starts every consult by asking: "is this a supply- or demand-constrained business?" ([yt-MH-IMJxbUY4 @ 4:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=296s))
3. **How your case fits.** Four people delivering client work is a supply constraint. Taking on more clients at today's price uses up your scarcest resource, your team's hours, without raising what each hour earns. He warns that owners often "fix a problem that's already a problem that if you fix it, makes your existing problem worse." ([yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4 @ 4:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=259s)) His answer when you have more demand than capacity: "when you have demand, cut supply" ([yt-uWdIgftpvBI @ 5:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=328s)).

**Why he'd say it**
- **A higher price can close more deals.** "if you raise your prices, what sometimes happens is that the conviction of the customer that you can actually deliver on the promise you're making goes up." ([yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4 @ 7:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=420s)) He adds that higher prices make clients less demanding: "you increase the emotional investment, you increase the perceived value, you increase the results, and you decrease the demandingness of the customer." ([@ 7:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=453s)) For a small team, less demanding clients matter as much as the extra revenue.
- **Use your close rate as the test.** "So whenever I hear 80% or over 80% close rates, I usually know that there's room in sale." In the HVAC example, the 10% raise paid off as long as "we close more than 65%" ([@ 8:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=486s)). If most prospects say yes, you're underpriced.
- **Sell to the clients who get the most out of your work.** "I do the same work to a business doing $100 million a year… 100x same work… solve rich people problems they pay better" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 1:38:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5918s)). For an agency, that means bigger clients, for whom a lift in results is worth more.
- **The middle is where people die.** "either sell extremely expensive stuff to a select few or sell something super cheap to everyone. The middle is where people die." ([yt-uWdIgftpvBI @ 0:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=0s)) A 4-person agency can't win on cheap volume, so go expensive.
- **Add a premium tier.** List an option at about 10x your normal price. A few buyers at that price add up, and even if nobody takes it, it makes your normal price look reasonable: "You have the expensive thing because even in tiny tiny volumes, lots of zeros still add up." ([yt-uWdIgftpvBI @ 9:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=587s))

**What he's done:** At a PR company in his portfolio, he noticed that the 15% of clients who bought the top package were the ones who stayed. He rebuilt the business to target only that kind of client and raised prices 10x, and response rates went up ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 1:23:11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=4991s)).

**What would change his answer**
- **Your team has spare capacity and leads are scarce.** Then you're demand-constrained. His order of fixes there is a better offer and better conversion, then more spend on the channel that already works, and only then a new channel.
- **Your close rate is already low**, or would drop below break-even after the raise. Then fix the offer before touching the price.
- **Your best clients start leaving and name price as the reason.** He has softened on this lately: he'll add a lower tier for ideal customers who say it's too expensive, but he still ignores price complaints from clients who aren't a good fit.

One note of my own, not his: try the new price on new clients first, then move existing retainers over gradually. He describes his own 10% raise as "more asking than telling."

Once I can read the vault, I'll answer the ads-vs-salesperson question with Hormozi's quotes and his reasoning, each linked to its source.

My guess without the vault: he'd probably say to put the money into paid ads first, plus a better offer and a tighter process for following up on leads. His usual point is that a salesperson only pays off once there are more leads than you can handle. I'll check that against what he actually says in the vault.

**Verdict:** Cut it down. Hormozi says that after price, overwhelm is the main reason members cancel, so adding more workouts and content would probably make your churn worse. Find the one thing your members actually use and value, make that excellent, and push the rest into the background.

**Based on:** said it. He talks directly about cancellations in membership and online-community businesses, and he gives a fitness example (Planet Fitness).

**Why he'd say it**
- **More content makes people cancel.** "The number one reason people churn, outside of price, is overwhelm. It is the churn driver. And this is why doing less can often retain more." ([How to Get Your Customers to Stay FOREVER, 2026-03 @ 9:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=558s))
- **Unused extras feel like wasted money.** "When you have five things that you pay for, but you only use one, you feel like you're only getting 20% of the value. If for the same price, you just offer that one thing, people feel like they're getting 100% of the value." ([@ 10:22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=622s)) He says adding features "gave them more reason to cancel because they never used it." ([@ 10:54](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=654s))
- **His test is subtraction.** "how much can I take away and still have it be good and not only be good but it probably is better" ([Less is More: The Magic of a Simple Business, 2025-05 @ 11:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=662s)). He calls complexity "the child of lazy thinking" ([@ 1:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=103s)).
- **Add things only when needed.** "you only introduce something when it's required or necessary for that person to get the the desired value" ([@ 11:35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=695s)).

**What he'd have you do**
1. **Find out why people actually leave.** Message everyone who cancels and tag the reason (price, overwhelm, not using it, not what they expected). "for every 20 cancels or so, review the top one or two reasons, and then fix those" ([@ 6:35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=395s)). Also ask your longest-staying members why they stay: "If you can only do one thing that gets people to stay, why would you do five?" ([@ 7:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=428s))
2. **Ask what members would keep.** "if I were to delete everything, what one thing would you fight for?" ([@ 11:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=686s)) Focus on the top one or two answers.
3. **Give busy members a simple path.** Think "value per second, not seconds of value" ([@ 12:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=720s)). For a fitness program, that means a "start here" plan and one clear workout schedule per week. Keep the extra library as optional "side quests" for the keen ones ([@ 12:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=753s)).
4. **Get new members an early win.** "pin the fast win up front so new members hit that value ideally within the first 24 hours" ([@ 13:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=786s)).
5. **Aim at day 90 and month 6.** Churn is highest in months 1–3, roughly halves after day 90, and falls to about 2% by month six. "Day 90 is probably going to have to deliver some sort of outcome, some sort of change in behavior for them. Month six, it's usually them connecting with other people within that community." ([@ 5:31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=331s)) For fitness, a visible result by about week 12 matters more than workout #47. His shortcut for month six is "get them to make one real friend" (@ 16:58).

**What he's done:** When overwhelm was the top reason people cancelled his Skool Games community, he cut live calls from three a week to one and moved the big monthly download to quarterly. He also turned off some app features ([@ 11:35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=695s)). At Gym Launch, gym owners asked to improve the product said they only wanted more leads. "if you just did the one thing that mattered, they wouldn't care about anything else" ([@ 14:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=859s)).

**What would change his answer:** if your tagged cancellation reasons turn out to be a missing feature, not overwhelm. Even then he'd add only that one thing, not more content in general. If your ideal members say price, he'd consider a cheaper tier or a discounted annual plan. Price complaints from people who aren't your target customer he'd ignore. He also warns: "don't overhaul your entire business because your month one churn sucks" ([@ 4:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=264s)). Fix the first month on its own before rebuilding everything.

The retention benchmarks come from Skool, a platform he's involved in. I can save this answer in the vault's `derived/` folder if you'd like to keep it.

**My best read until then (not in the vault, from what's generally known of Hormozi, no quotes):**

**Verdict:** He'd tell you to offer a guarantee, not a no-refunds policy. Ideally it would be a conditional guarantee tied to the client doing the work.

- In *$100M Offers*, risk reversal is one of the main ways to raise perceived value: it increases how likely the buyer feels the result is. At $2,000, a guarantee usually lifts sales by more than it costs you in refunds.
- He prefers **conditional** guarantees for coaching. For example: "attend every call, finish the assignments, and if you haven't hit X in 90 days, you get your money back," or "we keep working with you for free until you do." That protects you from people who buy and then do nothing. It also pushes clients to follow through, which gets them better results.
- His bigger point: if you're nervous about offering a guarantee, the problem is probably the program's results or who you're letting in. Fix that rather than hiding behind no refunds.

**What would change his answer:** If clients can take everything of value right away, like a course they can download, he'd lean toward a conditional or service-style guarantee rather than an unconditional refund.

I checked the vault's pages on debt, personal finance and his overall thinking, plus the raw transcripts.

**Verdict:** Pay off the car loan and the credit cards first. Then put what's left into the business, a bit at a time, on things that pay back fast. Don't put the whole $50k into the business while you still carry that debt.

His reasoning: cash only lets you take risk once you're "out of the hole." Every debt payment you get rid of is monthly cash flow you can put at risk later, without the worry in the back of your mind.

**Based on:** something he said, for the car. For the credit cards and the "don't go all in" part, it follows from what he said (high confidence).

**Why he'd say it**
- **On the car, he answered directly:** "ideally just pay off your car so you don't have to think about it again." In the same talk he says "ideally a paid-off clunker is the best way to go." ([First $100K video @ 2:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=128s))
- **On debt, he leans toward Dave Ramsey:** "I tend to skew like very close to the Ramsey side." His one argument: "Risk when multiplied over a long time horizon tends to come due," because "businesses have seasons, they have volatility." ([$2.5M consult @ 8:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=517s) / [9:10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=550s)) He never mentions credit cards in the vault, but consumer debt is a clearer case for that rule than the business debt he was talking about.
- **Get safe first, take risks second.** "The first step is that we have to cut all costs, so that we can take more risk." ([@ 0:32](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=32s)) Also: "get yourself out of the hole as fast as humanly possible. Like do whatever you got to do to get your oxygen mask on." ([15 Brutal Truths @ 17:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=1073s))
- **He doesn't say "never invest in the business."** Once you're stable, he wants the money spent on tools, one-on-one help and "trial attempts" such as ads, which he calls "minor investments that will give you huge leverage on your time." ([@ 11:25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=685s)) That means small bets you can measure, not one big lump sum.

**What he's done**
- An HVAC owner told him they planned to pay off $60k of business debt in 4–5 months. Hormozi said "Okay, good," and made "continue to pay off the debt" the #2 priority, right after a price raise ([@ 30:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=1845s)).
- When he had lost nearly everything in 2016, he seems to have funded a "hail Mary" with a credit card that had a $100k limit. The auto-captions are garbled there. It didn't come through, and he told Leila she should probably leave him ([Diary of a CEO @ 22:25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=1345s)). It's his own story of borrowed money nearly sinking him.

**What would change his answer**
- **The business already has proven returns.** His other rule is to spend "as much money as humanly possible" on ads while customer cost and return on ad spend hold steady. If you know $1 in reliably brings $3 back, he'd push you to fund that. Even then, the HVAC owner kept paying down debt while scaling ads, so he'd want both done, not debt left in place.
- **The debts are small next to the $50k.** Then paying them off is cheap, and he'd tell you to do it and move on.

Outside the vault: credit card rates are usually 20% or more, so paying them off is a guaranteed return few business bets can beat. That supports his view, but it's my point, not his.

Hormozi leans toward risk in general, but debt is the one area where he doesn't, and he admits his view is "more of an emotional thing." If you tell me roughly how much you owe and what the business does, I can work through how he'd split the $50k.

**Verdict:** He'd tell you to start with short-form clips, post a lot of them on every platform, and let the numbers show you what works. The clips that win then become your ads. The vault never has him compare long-form to short-form, though. What he does say is that bad content fails in any format.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). It rests on one close case, a 2026 consult where he told a business owner to grow through short-form, and on his volume rule, which shows up in three sources.

**How we get there**
1. **The nearest case.** In a 2026 consult, a travel-coaching founder said their short-form growth was "very painful and slow." Hormozi didn't tell them to switch formats. He said to fix how the clips were made, and to post more of them: "the best way to test this out is start getting more aggressive with your short-form content" ([yt-MH-IMJxbUY4 @ 13:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=786s)).
2. **The rule behind it.** His thinking page lists "do so much volume that failing would be unreasonable" and "let the market and tests decide, not his own taste." Short-form gives you the most attempts and the fastest feedback.
3. **Your case.** You want an audience for a business, which is the same goal that founder had. Both rules point toward the format you can make often, test cheaply and reuse as ads.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Volume across every platform.** This is how he describes his own content system: "if we post multiple times a day on every platform we'll get even more eyeballs so let's do that let's build that system" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 49:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=2966s)).
- **Test a batch every week and keep the winners.** "every week we just blast off 30 videos up there and we see where the winners are." ([yt-MH-IMJxbUY4 @ 8:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=523s))
- **Winning clips become ads.** "when you find your winners, just take that same post, add a 5-second CTA at the end, and then run that as an ad." He calls this a double dip: the post grows your audience, and it also tests your ad before you spend any money on it ([@ 13:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=820s)).
- **Quality beats format.** "good video beats images, but images beat bad videos" ([@ 10:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=656s)). He says the same about content in general: good content works and bad content doesn't. If your clips flop, he'd blame how they're made, not the format.
- **Hire someone who lives on the platform.** "You need to just get one hyper-caffeinated uh 20-year-old who lives and is brain-rotted Gen Z." ([@ 11:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=688s)) That person should copy the viral formats in your niche, use trending audio and shoot in a casual selfie style rather than a polished one.
- **A clip that flops still teaches you something.** "You post this content, nothing happens. That is still feedback." ([yt-jfW6gL6hKhk @ 9:48](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=588s))
- **Give it all away for free.** His content goal is to give "more value to a company before they've ever spoken to us" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 2:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=172s)).

**What he's done:** He built his own content as a system to post several times a day on every platform. He also makes long YouTube videos; all 13 sources in the vault are long-form. So in practice he does both, though the vault never has him explain how he splits them.

**Not in the vault:** Outside the vault, he's widely known for recording long-form material and cutting it into many short clips, with long-form building trust and clips bringing reach. If that's right, his full answer is "both, with clips for growth," not "short instead of long." None of the 13 sources says this, so treat it as unconfirmed.

**What would change his answer:**
- **A business that isn't visual.** His short-form advice was for a travel business, and he said it's "tougher" for something like tax savings, where you'd need an emotional angle instead.
- **A long-form channel that already works.** His rule is to improve the channel you have before adding a new one ("New channel, little too hard for right now"). In that case he'd say to make the long videos better first and start cutting clips from them.

The vault has no page on content formats, so this is the weakest part of the answer.

**Verdict:** Keep full price. If you want a Black Friday push, offer bonuses for a limited time with a deadline you actually enforce, not 30% off.

The vault never has Hormozi talking about Black Friday or percentage-off sales, so this is worked out from his pricing and offer rules. Those rules all point the same way. For him a higher price raises the buyer's belief that you'll deliver, so a markdown lowers it. When too few people buy, he says to make the offer better, not cheaper.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). Several of his stated rules apply, but none of them is about discounting a course specifically.

**How we get there**
1. **The closest thing he has addressed is raising prices, not cutting them.** Talking about a service business, he says *"if you raise your price, you increase the emotional investment, you increase the perceived value, you increase the results, and you decrease the demandingness of the customer."* ([yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4 @ 7:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=453s)). He also says *"they're so afraid of charging money that they actually sell themselves out of a sale"* (same source, @ 7:33).
2. **The rule behind it** ([[thinking/hormozi]]): charge more and sell to whoever values it most. *"some of the biggest levers that exist in the business is simply charging more because people actually believe you can deliver the service now."* ([yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4 @ 8:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=486s))
3. **How it applies to you:** a course works the same way. Whether someone buys depends on whether they believe it will get them the result. A 30% markdown runs his "virtuous cycle of pricing" backwards: buyers are less invested, so they get worse results, which weakens your proof for the next launch.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Fix the offer, not the price.** *"if we can't get enough people to say yes we need to make the offer better"* ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 1:25:23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5123s)). His value equation has four levers: dream outcome, perceived likelihood of achievement, time delay, and effort. Price isn't one of them. Urgency and scarcity are what he adds on top to make an offer more valuable.
- **Urgency only works if it's real.** *"the key to making urgency and scarcity work is making it legitimate"* and *"it means you say no and you say no so you can maintain the reputation"* ([yt-JDR-R--4HhM @ 21:50 / 22:29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=1310s)). He warns that once your audience learns the deadline doesn't matter, *"that's where you start losing power"* (@ 23:05). A yearly 30%-off sale teaches buyers to wait for November instead of buying now.
- **A reason helps, and Black Friday is a ready-made one.** *"you get bonus points for a reason if you can tie it back to urgency or scarcity"* ([yt-JDR-R--4HhM @ 10:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=633s)). So use the date as your reason for a time-limited bonus, not for a lower price.
- **He only answers price complaints when the evidence says to.** *"if your ideal customer say the price is the issue, then you can add a lower tier... If non-ideal people say it's too expensive, just ignore it. That means that the price is actually acting as a good filter"* ([yt--j8_YCWZ05Q @ 8:46](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=526s)). Even then his answer is a permanent cheaper tier, not a temporary sale.
- **The one discount he does endorse buys something back.** He recommends a discount of about 16–17% on annual plans, because buyers commit up front and churn less (same source, @ 15:52). A Black Friday markdown on a one-time course gets you no commitment in return.

**The math he'd make you do (my extrapolation, using his break-even method):** At 30% off, you need about 1.43× as many buyers just to bring in the same revenue. That's the same check he ran with "as long as we close more than 65%, we make more money" (@ 8:06), just run in the other direction. If you can't credibly expect 43% more sales, plus whatever full-price buyers you lose later because they learned to wait, the sale loses you money.

**What he'd tell you to do instead:** Keep the price. Add one or two bonuses that make the outcome come faster or easier, such as a live Q&A, templates, or a fast-start session. Run them for a fixed window that ends when you say it ends. Then actually close it and refuse late buyers.

**What would change his answer:**
- If your *ideal* buyers are telling you the price is the problem, he'd add a lower tier, still not run a sale.
- If the course barely converts at all, the problem is the offer, and a discount won't fix it.

**Outside the vault:** in *$100M Offers*, Hormozi argues for adding bonuses and value instead of discounting. The vault doesn't contain that book, so I haven't quoted it.

**Verdict:** The vault suggests Hormozi wouldn't promote your best rep just because they sell the most. He'd give the manager job to whoever has already proven they can do *that* job, which usually means someone from outside who has run a sales team and hit numbers. He'd keep your best rep selling, as the person the others learn from. If your team is still around five reps or fewer, he'd probably say you don't need a manager yet. You'd track the numbers yourself.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: **low–medium**). The vault has no source where he discusses promoting a rep versus hiring a manager. The answer comes from his general rules plus one similar case: a roofing company with a small sales team.

**How we get there**
1. **The similar case.** A roofing owner had four or five people and was hiring a salesperson. Hormozi didn't tell him to add a manager. He told the owner to track sales more closely himself, and said the next step comes once the team grows: "from a sales perspective, you're going to probably have to track this maybe a little bit more" ([yt-o64cI6tebnU @ 21:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=1274s)). **Verdict:** Keep running it, unless you've already decided you want out. A 3x profit offer means the buyer gets their money back in about three years and keeps everything after that, so you'd be trading a compounding asset for one lump sum. That only makes sense if selling was already your goal.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). The vault has no source where Hormozi talks about valuation multiples or whether to accept an offer. This answer applies his rules to your case.

**How we get there**
1. **The nearest thing he said.** When he consults on a business, one of the first things he asks the owner is what they want it to be: "Do you want to double it? Do you want to sell the business? Or do you just want to make money with it?" ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=263s) @ 4:23). That's his deciding question here. If you didn't plan to sell before this offer arrived, an offer alone isn't a reason to.
2. **The rule behind it.** His most consistent value is compounding over a long time instead of shortcuts. He says to stick with one path for a decade, and that "the effort that it takes to compound is the length of time you have to say no to everything else" ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=1378s) @ 22:58). He also says "Poor people stay poor because they want a fast way to get rich." ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sL16tsGafcQ) @ 0:00)
3. **Why your case falls under it.** If the business is healthy, about three years of profit now is the shortcut, and the compounding goes to the buyer. The cash would also move you from running a business to investing it. He calls investing "by far the slowest" path and says "almost no one makes their money this way" ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sL16tsGafcQ&t=852s) @ 14:12).

**Why he'd say it**
- **Risk is what gets paid.** "you will be compensated in proportion to the risk you're willing to take" ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rMJIOK_FgJk&t=463s) @ 7:43). Selling hands the risk, and the reward that comes with it, to the buyer. He also says "People will be willing to give you way more money than you think the risk is really worth cuz people are always afraid" (@ 15:19). A buyer paying only 3x is getting paid well for carrying that risk.
- **If the price is low, raise the business's value instead of selling.** He says that making revenue recurring "takes the business from being onetime business to recurring business, which is obviously significantly more valuable and dramatically increases LTV" ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=853s) @ 14:13). Applied to you: before selling, work on the things that make the company worth more.

**What he's done:** He sold 66% of Gym Launch and Prestige Labs at a $46.2M valuation in 2021. He kept a third and used the cash to start Acquisition.com. Afterwards he and his wife ran only a family office, which he calls "the most chill" period of his life. Still, he says: "Why am I back doing this when I don't need to do it anymore?" He went back to operating. So he did sell, but only part of the company, after years of building it, and with enough money to put into his next path.

**What would change his answer:**
- **You want out.** Selling was already your goal, or you're done with this business and have a clear next thing.
- **Safety comes first.** His rule is to cut costs and bank cash before taking big swings, because "Risk when multiplied over a long time horizon tends to come due" ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=550s) @ 9:10). If nearly all your net worth sits in this business, or it depends on one fragile channel, cashing out could be the right call. A partial sale, like his, would let you secure money and keep some upside.

**Where I disagree with him:** 3x profit is a normal price for a small business that depends on its owner. Whether this offer is low depends on how much the business needs you, so compare it with real offers for similar businesses before you decide.

([@ 5:23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=323s)), and "if nobody knows about your stuff, they can't give you money." ([@ 4:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=289s)). Learning to code would be a second skill competing with your one main bet: "The price of wanting to be good at everything is being good at nothing." ([15 Brutal Truths @ 22:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=1344s))
4. **Getting other people to do the work is a step up in leverage.** "first I was working for someone else then I worked for myself then I got other people to work for me first level each of those levels was more leverage" ([Diary of a CEO @ 1:44:41](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=6281s)). Writing the code yourself puts you back on the lower rung.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Find the constraint first.** In every consult he starts by asking whether the business is limited by supply or by demand ([thinking page](vaults/hormozi/wiki/thinking/hormozi.md)). For most small businesses the limit is demand, and an app doesn't fix demand.
- **Hire expertise rather than struggle alone.** "The fastest way to learn skills is to find somebody who's really good and hire them one-on-one." ([First $100K @ 9:48](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=588s))
- **Cheap builds create technical debt.** When you bootstrap with low-quality software, "you're going to have some technical debt" ([4 Paths to Wealth @ 4:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sL16tsGafcQ&t=292s)).

**What he's done:** He bootstrapped ALAN, a lead-handling software company for agencies, which he says reached $1.7M a month within six months. He started it only after he already had a gym-owner customer base and the cash from Gym Launch and Prestige Labs. Software came after the demand, not before.

**What would change his answer:**
- **The app *is* the business.** If you're building a software product, coding is your core skill. His advice then flips to doing high volume yourself ("10,000 iterations") or bringing on a strong technical person.
- **You have almost no cash.** His rule is to cut costs first. In that case, a scrappy version you build yourself with AI tools fits his idea of a cheap "trial attempt": a test to prove demand, not a new career.

My own view, separate from his: AI coding tools have made a DIY prototype much cheaper than when he made most of these statements. A weekend prototype to test demand is reasonable. Building and maintaining a production app yourself is still the trap his reasoning warns against.
